scenes.narration: The three-bit file scored forty-one versus thirty-nine point eight for the full-size original on DeepSWE. DeepSWE is a benchmark where an agent must solve real software tasks. Every earlier file below three bits solved at most seventy-two percent of the original's tasks.

Quantization, storing each number in fewer bits, is like writing pi as three point one and dropping the tail. NariQ's trick is trellis coding, a rounding scheme that remembers earlier roundings, so small errors cancel instead of stacking. Think of an MP3 next to its studio master. The limit is that the loss is uneven: exact math notices first, casual chat never does.

What actually shipped is a GGUF, the one-file format your local tools load, at ten point one two gigabytes. The catch sits in the fine print, where catches live. The scores came from Nari Labs' own fork of llama.cpp, a modified engine tuned for workstation silicon. Stock llama.cpp cannot open it yet, and on other hardware it runs slower.

scenes.narration: The original stores every number as BF16, the model's full sixteen-bit memory. NariQ stores the same numbers in three bits. That is about a fifth of the space each, and that shrinking, not new intelligence, removes the memory wall.

Now the honest limits. These numbers are four days old, and Nari Labs graded its own homework in its own harness. GeForce cards have not been tested yet. And the runtime runs slower than stock quants except on one workstation GPU.
The myth still holds where precision bites. Long stretches of exact math expose the flattening. If you chase the last fraction of a point, the full-size original is still your tool.
At three bits, the question stops being whether the model is good enough. It becomes what memory you have.
